cards.title: 1.1.1 What is Biology?
body: The word “biology” is derived from two Greek words: “bios” meaning “life” and “logos” meaning “study of”.
Biology is therefore the branch of science that deals with the study of life or living things.
All living things are often called organisms.
An organism is a living entity consisting of one cell such as bacteria or several cells like animals, plants and fungi.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Branches of Biology
body: The study of biology can be divided into different branches.
Biology often overlaps with other sciences such as biochemistry and biogeography.
In studying biology, one acquires very useful knowledge that can be used in many ways.
To develop the scientific skills such as observation, identifying, recording, classifying, measuring, analyzing and evaluating.

1.2.1 Cell Theory
body: A cell is the structural and functional unit of all organisms.
Cells vary in size, shape, and function.
Most cells cannot be seen with the unaided eye.
The smallest cells are bacteria and the biggest cells are birds’ eggs.

cards.title: 1.2.2 The Cell Structure
body: A nucleus is a membrane-bound structure where deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is housed within thread-like structures called chromosomes.
Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) This is a network of interconnected tubules.
One of the most important functions of this organelle is the synthesis of lipids.
Golgi Apparatus This is an organelle consisting of membrane-bound sacks that modify the products of the ER and then transport them to other organelles or to the cell surface.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
body: Eukaryotic cells are much more complex and in general larger than prokaryotic cells.
Prokaryotic cells are those cells found in bacteria.
The most obvious difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells is the presence of a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.
A prokaryotic cell lacks a true nucleus.

cards.title: 1.3.1 Permeability
body: Among the cell’s most important activities is its interaction with the environment.
Without this process life cannot persist.
The cell membrane takes up substances the cell needs such as oxygen and glucose, and disposes of the cell’s wastes such as carbon dioxide and excess water.
The cell membrane exhibits selective permeability.

cards.title: 1.3.2 The Transportation of Molecules
body: All living organisms need to transport useful materials into the cells and remove waste materials from the cells in order to carry out their life activities.
Diffusion is the movement of particles from a high concentration to a low concentration until they are spread out evenly.
Particles move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration through a semi-permeable membrane or through the air.
Because a cell does not required energy when molecules diffuse across the membrane, the diffusion of a substance across a biological membrane is called passive transport.

cards.title: 1.3.3 Homeostasis
body: In order to remain alive, cells must maintain a biological balance with their immediate environment.
Cells undergo homeostasis by controlling and regulating what passes in and out of them.
Though cells can exist within a range of environmental states, there is a limit to how much they can adjust to.
Homeostasis is dynamic and is affected by environmental changes.

cards.title: 1.3.4 Respiration
body: All living things require energy to survive.
Whether they are unicellular or multicellular, all organisms need energy to undergo cellular activities.
Cells are constantly active in building, repairing, growing and reproducing activities, which require energy.
During aerobic respiration, sugar is combined with oxygen and energy is released.

cards.title: 1.3.5 Excretion
body: Chemical reactions constantly take place inside living cells.
The sum total of all chemical reactions carried out by the cell is called metabolic reactions or metabolism.
The byproducts of metabolism are considered waste products because they are unwanted by the cells and need to be removed.
Carbon dioxide and water, produced from cellular respiration, and nitrogenous compounds, produced from the break down of proteins, are the main waste products that the body must eliminate.

cards.title: 1.4.1 The Structures and Forms of Bacteria
body: Cell Wall Most bacteria possess relatively rigid, protective outer cell walls that give the cells their characteristic shape.
The cell wall is composed of proteins and carbohydrates called the peptidoglycan layer.
The possession of peptidoglycan layer makes the cell wall of bacteria different from the cell wall of plants (remember, the cell wall of plants is made up of cellulose).
The capsule protects the cell from the host’s immune defenses, and serves as a means of attachment to the cell surfaces of the host during infection.

cards.title: 1.4.2 The Economic Importance of Bacteria
body: Although considered structurally simple, bacteria are extremely diverse in terms of their metabolic processes and are found almost everywhere on earth in vast numbers.
Humans and all other organisms depend on bacteria in many ways.

Beneficial bacteria are involved in such diverse processes as digestion in animals, nitrogen fixation in the roots of certain legumes, the decomposition of animal and plant remains, and sewage disposal systems.
Pathogenic bacteria, on the other hand, can cause severe and often fatal diseases in humans, animals and plants.

cards.title: 1.5.1 The Structures of Viruses
body: Most viruses are much smaller than bacteria.
The complete assembly of an infectious particle is known as a virion.
A virion is a nucleic acid (DNA or RNA not both) core surrounded by a protein coat or capsid.
Lipids provide flexibility to the shape of these viruses.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Comparison with Cells
body: The nature of viruses is ambiguous whether they are living organisms or non-living matter.
Once inside the host, some viruses may remain dormant for long periods, causing no obvious change in their host cells.
The virus stays in this dormant stage until there is change in the host cell, which then leads to the formation of new viruses.
New viruses are then assembled and burst out of the host cell (i.e. killing the cell) to infect other cells.

cards.title: 1.5.3 Diseases Caused by Viruses
body: Smallpox, the common cold, chickenpox, influenza, shingles, herpes, polio, rabies, Ebola and HIV/AIDS are some of the examples of viral diseases in humans.
HIV/AIDS Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is a disease that develops when people are infected with the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
Human Immunodeficiency Virus is dangerous because it specifically attacks the white blood cells, which normally are used to fight the virus itself.
Once HIV kills sufficient white blood cells, the infection slowly progresses to AIDS.

DNA contains Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), and Cytosine (C).

**Step 2: Identify bases present in RNA**

**Step 3: Compare differences**
Uracil replaces Thymine in RNA.

**Final Result:**
**Uracil** is unique to RNA.

units.title: Taxonomy
units.intro:
Classification groups living things so we can name, compare and study them. **Binomial:** Genus species (Homo sapiens) — italic or underlined. Keys: paired choices (dichotomous) to identify a specimen.

**Five kingdoms** in this book: Monera (bacteria, prokaryote), Protista (mostly unicellular eukaryotes), Fungi (heterotroph, chitin wall, spores), Plantae (multicellular, cellulose, photosynthesise), Animalia (multicellular, ingest food, no wall).

cards.title: 2.1 The Importance of Classification
body: From early times humans have found it convenient to classify plants and animals according to their usage, habit or size.
For example plants can be classified according to their use as edible, poisonous or medicinal plants.
According to their characteristics plants can be divided into herbs, shrubs, and trees.
The branch of biology that deals with the naming and classification of organisms is called taxonomy.
A biologist who specializes in this field of study is called a taxonomist.

cards.title: 2.3.1 Kingdom Monera
body: All members of the kingdom monera are prokaryotic and unicellular.
The kingdom includes organisms like bacteria and cyanobacteria (formerly known as blue-green algae).
Bacteria are simple and most abundant microorganisms.
Mode of Nutrition The means whereby an organism assimilates its food is called nutrition.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Kingdom Protista
body: Kingdom protista includes many simple eukaryotes.
All are aerobic and have mitochondria for cellular respiration.
Most of them reproduce or grow by binary fission and conjugation.
Many can form cysts (an outer covering) in adverse conditions.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Kingdom Fungi
body: Fungi are filamentous eukaryotes with a saprophytic mode of nutrition.
Fungal filaments are known as hyphae and a mass of hyphae is called a mycelium (plural: mycelia).
Fungi are very important in the environment as decomposers.
Fungi reproduce both asexually and sexually by spore formation.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Kingdom Plantae
body: Members of the kingdom plantae are multicellular eukaryotes that have cell walls made of cellulose.
Plants store their food in the form of starch.
The life cycle of plants is a complex alternation of generations.
In the life cycle, the sporophyte generation alternates with the gametophyte generation.

cards.title: 2.3.5 Kingdom Animalia
body: All animals are composed of eukaryotic cells.
A fundamental aspect of the organization of an animal body is the body shape, form, and manner in which the body parts are arranged.
A structure that allows an animal to be divided into parts of an equal shape and size, and a similar position to the line of division is called symmetry.
Symmetry is used to describe the arrangement of body structures with reference to the body axis.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Carbohydrates
body: Carbohydrates are the most abundant organic compounds in living organisms.
Based on the sugar units they contain, carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, disaccharides or polysaccharides.
Carbohydrates are mainly found in plants such as potatoes, rice and wheat.
Monosaccharides are single sugar containing molecules.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Lipids
body: The word lipid comes from the Greek word “lipos”, meaning “fat” or “lard” (fat of pork/a pig).
Like carbohydrates, lipids are large molecules made up of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
The most common lipids are fats, oils and waxes.
Lipids are found in animals and plants e.g. butter and groundnut oil.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Proteins
body: Protein molecules are made up of long chains of smaller molecules joined end to end.
Amino acids are classified as essential or non-essential amino acids.
Essential amino acids are those which cannot be synthesized by the body.
Non-essential amino acids are those that the body can synthesize from other amino acids or nutrients present in food.

cards.title: 3.1.4 Nucleic acids
body: The two nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) vary in some of their structural components and in their functions.
Deoxyribonucleic acid contains deoxyribose and ribonucleic acid contains ribose.
Deoxyribonucleic acid is a long molecule made up of two strands of materials, which are twisted into a shape called a double helix.
The double helix looks like a ladder that has been twisted into a spiral staircase.

units.intro:
**Adaptation** is a feature that helps survival and reproduction in a habitat. Not “the animal wanted it.”

**Plants:** cold — short season, dwarf, dark leaves sometimes. Drought — small/waxy leaves, sunken stomata, deep or wide roots, water store (cactus). Salt — salt glands, succulence. Wind — flexible stems, small leaves. Eritrea highland vs coastal desert is the local pair to use in essays.

cards.title: 4.1 What is Adaptation?
body: Living organisms are characterized by the changes they make to live in the environmental conditions around them.
The changes can be morphological (change in structure and form) or physiological (internal and functional change), and is called adaptation.
Adaptation is the modification in structure or function that increases the fitness of an organism in a stressful environment.
Adaptation is hereditary and thus passed from one generation to the next.
Adaptation mechanisms of living organisms to various environmental stress factors are generally classified as avoidance, tolerance and escape mechanisms.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Adaptations of Plants to Temperature
body: Temperature is a very important environmental factor that affects plant functions and growth.
At low temperatures, plants develop adaptations that allow them to reduce their exposure to the cold environment.
Transpiration is the loss of water from plants through the small openings called stomata in the leaves and stems.
The low temperature limits soil water uptake.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Adaptations of Plants to Water
body: Plants are classified into three major categories according to their adaptations to water conditions.
The majority of plant species live in optimal environments with regard to water availability.
Mesophytes are plants that live under normal water conditions or in intermediate water availability e.g. many crop species.
Mesophytes usually have a well developed root system, their leaves are flat and their stomata do not have protective features.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Adaptations of Plants to Salt
body: Plants such as mangroves, that cover a great part of the seashores in Massawa and the coastal areas, are salt-tolerant plants.
Mangroves also have small openings (lenticels) in their bark that allow oxygen to diffuse into the plant and down into its underground roots.
Many salt-tolerant plants have developed salt glands, salt-filtering root, or salt-excreting leaves or branches in order to prevent the build up of high salt concentrations.
Mangroves for example almost completely eliminate salt and, when squeezed, their leaves consist of almost pure water.

**Step 1: Define the structural layers of a leaf**
*   Stomata: breathing pores.
*   Epidermis: outermost cell layer.
*   Aerenchyma: air-storing tissue in water plants.
*   Cuticle: waxy, waterproof non-cellular outer layer that minimizes water loss.

**Final Result:**
**Cuticle**.

glossary.meaning: Plants that have developed adaptations to saline environments are called halophytes.
Hibernation: This is a type of long-term metabolic rate reduction in cold weather.
Adaptation is the modification in structure or function that increases the fitness of an organism in a stressful environment.
Temperature is a very important environmental factor that affects plant functions and growth.
Transpiration is the loss of water from plants through the small openings called stomata in the leaves and stems.

tips.text: Plants are classified into mesophytes, hydrophytes and xerophytes, according to the adaptations they have developed in response to water conditions.
